Classifying camera trap images with machine learning needs many images of known species.
WildObs records the species in every image of an observation, so its openly hosted images
come labelled. This vignette finds those images, joins them to their labels, and downloads a
small batch. It uses a 2023 University of Queensland teaching survey at Dwyers Scrub,
Queensland, most of whose images are hosted by WildObs.


``` r
library(WildObsR)

# your personal API key, read from .Renviron (see the Get started vignette)
api_key <- Sys.getenv("WILDOBSR_API_KEY")

# the project, with its media table
id <- "QLD_Dwyers_Scrub_ANIM3018_2023_WildObsID_0005"
dp <- wildobs_dp_download(api_key = api_key, project_ids = id, media = TRUE)[[id]]
media <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "media")
```

## Which images can be downloaded

Most WildObs images stay with the people who collected them, or with Wildlife Insights.
Only images with `filePublic = TRUE` are openly hosted by WildObs, and only those can be
downloaded. The rest are listed, with their timestamps and labels, but their `filePath`
reads `not_publicly_accessible`, and file names are withheld from public users.


``` r
# images in this project that WildObs hosts openly
table(media$filePublic)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>  3678 17832
```

Across the whole public database the share of openly hosted images is small, so check
`filePublic` before planning a training set.

## Label each image with its species

Each media row carries the `observationID` it belongs to, a WildObs addition to Camtrap DP.
Joining on it gives every image the species, count and observation type recorded for that
observation:


``` r
# the observations, read with their schema types
obs <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "observations")
# the label columns of each observation
labels <- obs[, c("observationID", "observationType", "scientificName", "count")]

# each public image with its label
public <- merge(media[media$filePublic, c("mediaID", "deploymentID", "observationID",
                                          "timestamp", "filePath")],
                labels, by = "observationID")

# how many labelled images of each kind
table(public$observationType)
#> 
#>       animal        human      vehicle        blank      unknown unclassified 
#>         8302           93            0         9437            0            0

# the species with the most openly hosted images
head(sort(table(public$scientificName[public$observationType == "animal"]),
          decreasing = TRUE), 8)
#> 
#>         Alectura lathami    Notamacropus dorsalis Notamacropus rufogriseus 
#>                     3450                      889                      832 
#>  Leucosarcia melanoleuca         Wallabia bicolor        Isoodon macrourus 
#>                      538                      361                      169 
#>             Macropodidae         Perameles nasuta 
#>                      163                      159
```

Projects differ in which images they host openly. This one also hosts blank images
(`observationType == "blank"`); keep some in a training set, because models must also learn
to say that nothing is there.

## Download a batch

`wildobs_media_download()` saves each file into a folder per project and deployment, skips
files already on disk, and reports what happened to each one. Start with a few files to
check the setup before downloading thousands:


``` r
# the two species with the most images
top <- names(sort(table(public$scientificName[public$observationType == "animal"]),
                  decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
# three labelled images of each, as a test batch
batch <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top, function(sp) {
  # the first three images of this species
  utils::head(public[public$scientificName %in% sp, ], 3)
}))

# download them into a temporary folder
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "wildobs_images")
result <- wildobs_media_download(batch, out_dir = out_dir)
#> 6 of 6 media files have a path that can be tried (6 web, 0 Google Cloud, 0 on this computer).
#> downloaded: 6

# what happened to each file, and where it went
table(result$downloadStatus)
#> 
#> downloaded 
#>          6
basename(result$localPath)
#> [1] "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_1.jpg"   "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_4.jpg"  
#> [3] "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_5.jpg"   "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_235.jpg"
#> [5] "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_225.jpg" "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_226.jpg"
```

The returned table keeps every column you passed in, so the labels stay with the files:
`result$scientificName` names the species in each `result$localPath`. Write it out with
the images, for example as `labels.csv`, and the batch is ready for training.

## Cite and credit

Images are licensed with their project, usually under a Creative Commons licence that
requires attribution. Check the media licence, and cite the project in any model or
dataset you publish:


``` r
# the licence that applies to this project's images
extract_metadata(dp, "licenses")[, c("name", "scope", "path")]
#>        name scope                                         path
#> 1 CC-BY-4.0  data https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
#> 2 CC-BY-4.0 media https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

# and the reference to cite
writeLines(cite_datapackages(dp))
#> Zachary Amir & Annabel Smith (2023). WildObs Camera Trap Data Package: UQ's undergraduate widlife techonologies camera trapping module comparing human and AI comptuer vision [Camera Trap Data Package]. WildObs National Wildlife Camera Database. https://wildobs.org.au. RAiD: https://raid.org/10.83062/a3efd562. WildObs database version 1.0.1.
```
